Watermelon Man for Congas

Watermelon Man is a 16-bar blues that a conga player can learn in an afternoon, once the tumbao is under the hands. If you have not played the tumbao yet, start with How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao. This page assumes the heel, toe, slap and open tones, and the part Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open.

How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the part written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a conga staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Congas alone to hear the congas without the bass and piano, and Leave out the congas to take over. Each step starts in its own style and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both. The sounds are General MIDI stand-ins, so the heel, toe, slap and bass tones are approximations: listen to a real player for the sound.

The tune and its history

Herbie Hancock wrote Watermelon Man for his first album, Takin’ Off (Blue Note, 1962), with Freddie Hubbard, Dexter Gordon, Butch Warren and Billy Higgins on drums. No conga player is listed on that record. It is in F, in even eighths: Hancock said Higgins played “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz”. It goes at roughly 120 to 130 beats a minute.

Late in 1962 Hancock filled in on piano in the band of the conga player Mongo Santamaría for a weekend at a club in the Bronx, and Donald Byrd urged him to play the tune for Mongo. Mongo’s band recorded it on 17 December 1962 “in a cha-cha beat”, with Kako Baster on timbales, Victor Venegas on bass and Ray Lucas adding a backbeat on drums. The single came out on Battle in 1963 and reached the top ten or eleven of the Billboard Hot 100 (sources differ). It is slower than Hancock’s, and is often named as a starting point of boogaloo and Latin soul. A much later remake, on Head Hunters in 1973, has Bill Summers blowing into beer bottles after the Central African hindewhu.

What this lesson teaches, and what it does not. No published transcription of the conga part on Mongo’s record was found. What you learn here is the standard tumbao, the part a conga player plays in a cha-cha beat. Listen to the record and copy what you hear.

Reading the part

Click a note head to hear that stroke. The conga is written on the top space; a low drum, when there is one, sits on a lower space. A plain head is the open tone (or the bass tone), an ✕ is the slap, a triangle is heel or toe, and a diamond is the muted tone. Two lines of words sit under the notes: the stroke (H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muted, B bass) and the hand (L or R).

The form

It is a 16-bar blues: a 12-bar blues whose bars 9 and 10 (C7 and B♭7) are played three times. In F, with one chord to a bar:

  • Bars 1 to 4: F7, F7, F7, F7
  • Bars 5 to 8: B♭7, B♭7, F7, F7
  • Bars 9 to 12: C7, B♭7, C7, B♭7
  • Bars 13 to 16: C7, B♭7, F7, F7

The Backing Track has the same form as its “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset, with the band stopping on bar 14 (the break). The steps below use it.

1. The form, with the open tones only

Start with the two open tones, on 4 and the and of 4, and nothing else. Count the sixteen bars out loud. Listen for the three C7 to B♭7 pairs in bars 9 to 14: that is the part of the form a 12-bar blues does not have.

2. The right hand

Add the slap on 2. The right hand plays the slap, then the two open tones. The slap on 2 lands with the backbeat.

3. The tumbao, slowly

Now the whole part: Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open, hands L L R L L L R R, one bar at a time, in a cha-cha beat at about 100 beats a minute. Do not speed up to catch the band; keep the left hand quiet and the slap and open tones clear.

4. The break

On bar 14 the band stops. The congas play one open tone on beat 1 with the band, then nothing, and come back in on bar 15 with the band. Count the silent beats. The two bars shown large are bars 13 and 14.

The bar after the stop is the hard part: nothing in the band tells you the time but your own counting. Say “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” out loud through bar 14.

5. With the melody

The tune, written in F, above the chart. The band plays it on the piano with the congas. Tick Leave out the tune to hear the congas and the band alone. In this step the band plays straight through the break, so the melody is not cut off.

Read the melody as you play. The riff in bars 1 and 2 is the line everyone knows.

6. Mongo’s way and Herbie’s way

The same part in two styles. The first plays the congas in the Cha-cha at a moderate tempo, as Mongo’s band recorded it, with the break on bar 14. The second is the Boogaloo at about 126, with straight eighths and the break, nearer Hancock’s own tempo. Change between them with the Feel menu at the bottom. The part is the same tumbao in both.

Mongo’s way: Cha-cha, a moderate tempo.

Herbie’s way: Boogaloo, about 126.

7. Two drums

As an extension, the same form with two drums in the Son montuno: every second bar the right hand plays two open tones on the low drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel. Which bar of the pair takes the low drum depends on the clave, and this lesson does not say which way the clave runs on the record. A one-bar tumbao avoids the question: stay with step 6 until you can play it through without thinking.

Where to go next

  • Play step 6 with the congas left out and the tumbao in your hands for ten choruses.
  • Learn the five strokes properly in How to Play Congas.
  • Blues for Drums has the same kind of steps for a drum kit.
  • Tools → Backing Track has the “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset and a Congas menu that works in any style.
  • Listen to Mongo Santamaría’s record and copy what you hear.
